whyWrong.C: The cylinder's capacity is mentioned, but the error the passage sets up is about interpretation of the performance, not about failing to notice the equipment's limits — noticing them is what would prevent the error.

commonMistakes: Picking the choice that repeats a detail from the passage instead of the one that names the reasoning error the details add up to.

whyCorrect: The passage gives two separate conditions. Good faith is one, and the buyer satisfies it. But the thing itself must also be capable of the benefit, and a stolen object is "permanently barred from it however long it was held and through however many hands it passed." That bar attaches to the object, so no state of mind on the buyer's part can cure it.

whyWrong.A: The land period applies to a category of thing, not to a defect of title; a stolen movable is excluded outright rather than made to wait longer.
whyWrong.B: Nothing in the passage concerns penalties, and the buyer is described as wholly innocent.
whyWrong.D: This applies the good-faith condition and ignores the second condition, which the passage says is absolute for stolen goods.

tips: When a rule carries two conditions, check the choice against both — most distractors satisfy one and quietly drop the other.

whyCorrect: "Two wars suspended that promise" is a complete sentence, and "The note that circulates today is legal tender because Parliament says so" is another. With no conjunction between them, the boundary must be a full stop (or a semicolon); of the options only the period is offered.

whyWrong.A: A colon is not paired with "and," and the second clause is not an explanation or list introduced by the first.
whyWrong.C: A comma between two independent clauses with no coordinating conjunction is a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation the sentences fuse, and "that promise note" reads momentarily as a single noun phrase.

tips: Test each side as a standalone sentence; when both pass and there is no conjunction, only a period or semicolon will do.

whyCorrect: Strip the sentence down: the subject is "A photographer who has coated six plates in an afternoon and has begun to see thin, patchy negatives" and the verb is "tests." The whole "who" clause is a restrictive modifier inside the subject, so nothing separates it from the verb that follows. The blank takes no punctuation.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides; "tests the strength of the bath" has no subject of its own.
whyWrong.B: A colon must follow a complete statement, and everything before the blank is only a noun phrase.
whyWrong.D: A comma here severs the subject from its verb, which Standard English does not permit however long the subject is.

commonMistakes: Adding a comma because a pause feels natural after a long subject — length is never the test, structure is.

whyCorrect: "A design whose mirror can be supported across the whole of its back" is an appositive renaming "the reflector," and it is already closed by the comma before "has no such limit." A non-essential appositive needs a comma at both ends, so the opening comma is required after "it."

whyWrong.A: Without the opening comma the appositive runs straight on from "replaced it," leaving the closing comma unmatched.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, but "a design whose mirror can be supported…" is a noun phrase.
whyWrong.D: A colon would announce the appositive as a specification and could not then be closed by the comma that follows; the sentence resumes with its main verb, so a paired comma is what fits.

tips: Look ahead for a comma later in the sentence — a lone closing comma tells you an opening one is missing.

whyCorrect: "That open on a rising fourth" identifies which four versions are meant out of the hundred and twelve, so it is a restrictive clause. A restrictive relative clause is never separated from the noun it limits, and "that" cannot follow a mark of punctuation here at all.

whyWrong.A: A comma before "that" would make the clause non-essential, but it is the only thing telling you which versions are grouped.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "that open on a rising fourth are placed together" cannot stand alone as a sentence.
whyWrong.C: A colon must follow a complete statement, and "The four versions" is only a noun phrase.

tips: A clause beginning with "that" is restrictive by definition — no comma before it.

whyCorrect: The clause after "and" has a subject, "that rotation," but no verb until the blank fills it. Only a finite verb can complete a clause, and the present tense "allows" agrees with the singular subject and matches the general present of the rest of the passage.

whyWrong.B: "To allow" is an infinitive, which cannot serve as the main verb of the clause, leaving "that rotation" with nothing to do.
whyWrong.C: "Having allowed" is a participle phrase, so the clause still has no finite verb.
whyWrong.D: "Allowing" is also a participle; it would turn the second half into a fragment hanging off the first.

tips: Find the subject after the conjunction and ask what its verb is — if the blank is the only candidate, it must be a finite verb.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with "Working through a long sequence of such moves," a participial phrase describing whoever did the working. The main clause must therefore begin with that person, and only this option supplies one: a student in the seminar.

whyWrong.A: "There" is an empty placeholder and names nobody who could have worked through the moves, so the phrase dangles.
whyWrong.B: This makes "the number of crossings" the thing doing the working, which is impossible — a number cannot perform moves.
whyWrong.D: This makes "it" — an anticipatory subject standing for the clause that follows — the worker, which again leaves the opening phrase without anyone to attach to.

tips: After an -ing opener, the first noun of the main clause has to be capable of performing that action.

whyCorrect: The passage is set in the 1880s and the surrounding verbs are past — the observatory "ran" on one engine, a failure "halted" the night's work. The verb in the blank must match that past frame, and the compound plural subject "The dome, the rising floor and the clock drive" takes the plural past form "drew."

whyWrong.A: "Is drawing" is singular and present progressive, clashing with both the plural subject and the historical setting.
whyWrong.B: "Draws" is singular present; the subject is three things and the time is the 1880s.
whyWrong.D: "Has drawn" is singular and present perfect, implying a period reaching the present, which the 1880s setting rules out.

commonMistakes: Letting the nearest noun, "the clock drive," decide the number instead of the full three-part subject.

whyCorrect: The first sentence limits the jurists to a small world — runaway slaves, boundary walls, the sale of oil. The second reports their reasoning being applied to banking and public authority, questions no Roman ever faced. The second happens despite the narrowness of the first, so the transition must be concessive.

whyWrong.A: "In other words" would make the medieval reception a restatement of the Roman subject matter, but it introduces a wholly different range of problems.
whyWrong.C: "Consequently" would make the later application follow from the narrowness of the original cases, which is the opposite of the relationship.
whyWrong.D: "For instance" would offer banking and public authority as examples of household and cattle cases, which they explicitly are not.

tips: When the second sentence names something the first would not lead you to expect, choose a concessive transition.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states the general point: a property surviving every permitted redrawing can distinguish two knots. The second gives one such property — the least number of crossings — and shows it doing exactly that job, separating a knot needing seven from one needing three. That is an illustration of the general claim.

whyWrong.A: "By contrast" requires opposition, but the crossing number is an instance of the property just described, not a counter to it.
whyWrong.C: "However" also signals contrast; the second sentence agrees with and exemplifies the first.
whyWrong.D: "In conclusion" marks a final summing-up, and this sentence introduces a specific new example rather than closing the argument.

tips: A general statement followed by one named case is nearly always an example transition.

whyCorrect: The first sentence shows the wheel defeating the gravity response, because a direction that keeps changing averages out. The second shows the same wheel failing to defeat the light response, because a lamp fixed at one side stays in one place. Same apparatus, opposite outcome, so the transition has to mark contrast.

whyWrong.A: "Likewise" claims the two cases behave the same way, but one response is abolished by the turning and the other is not.
whyWrong.B: "In short" introduces a summary, and the second sentence adds a new and different result.
whyWrong.D: "Consequently" would make the shoot's bending follow from the root's straight growth; the two are independent responses with different causes.

commonMistakes: Seeing the same wheel in both sentences and assuming the results must agree.

whyCorrect: The goal has two parts — what the measurement leaves out, and how the soak supplies it — so the answer must carry both. This choice names the gap (strength recorded, phase not, though both are needed) and then the remedy (dense atoms altering the recorded strengths in a way that yields the phases).

whyWrong.A: This states what is needed but never mentions the heavy-metal soak, so it explains no remedy.
whyWrong.C: This names the missing quantity only. The half of the goal about how it is recovered is absent.
whyWrong.D: This describes the soak but stops before saying what it does about the missing phases.

tips: When the goal names a problem and a fix, count both in your choice before selecting it.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why this proof was received differently, so the answer must name what set it apart. This choice supplies it: the argument was complete, but it rested on about 1,500 configurations checked by machine, and no mathematician had read the whole of that checking. A proof no human can verify in full is exactly what made the reception unusual.

whyWrong.B: This states the conjecture. It says nothing about the proof or its reception.
whyWrong.C: This gives the reduction to 1,500 configurations but leaves out the computer checking and the unread verification, which are what made it controversial.
whyWrong.D: That the conjecture was long unproved is background; many long-standing results are proved without any change in how proofs are received.

commonMistakes: Choosing a note about the proof's achievement rather than the feature that made mathematicians uneasy about it.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why the method depended on glassmaking, so the answer must run the causal chain from method to pressure to glass. This choice does it: fermentation sealed in the bottle traps the gas, the finished bottle stands at about six atmospheres, that pressure burst much of every early cellar, and only the stronger coal-fired English glass could hold it.

whyWrong.A: This states the losses without explaining what produced the pressure or which glass solved it, so the dependence is left unexplained.
whyWrong.B: This describes the better glass alone. Nothing connects it to the fermentation method or the pressure involved.
whyWrong.D: This gives the first step of the chain only and never reaches the glass.

tips: A "why did X depend on Y" goal needs every link between X and Y, not just the two endpoints.

whyCorrect: The frame "____ rather than false" needs a word meaning incomplete but not wrong. The passage lists three things the notation cannot spell — a flattened third, a line let fall away, a beat held longer than the bar — and says whatever he could not spell left the record. What he did write is accurate as far as it goes and simply missing the rest: partial.

whyWrong.A: Nobody in the passage contests the transcriptions; the limitation is in the notation, not in any disagreement about them.
whyWrong.C: They are perfectly readable — that is the point of using standard notation. The failure is in what the notation cannot represent.
whyWrong.D: Authorship is not in question anywhere in the text.

tips: With "____ rather than false," find the word that names a shortfall short of error, and check the passage for what was left out.

whyCorrect: The colon explains the blank: the cart rocks on rough ground, and the cone braces the wheel against the thrust that rocking sends along the axle. The shape does a job, so it is chosen on purpose — contradicting the impression that the wheel looks half-collapsed to an untrained eye.

whyWrong.A: Nothing suggests the coned shape is a stage on the way to something else; it is how the wheel is built and stays.
whyWrong.B: "Unavoidable" would mean the builder had no choice, but the passage describes a design that answers a specific load.
whyWrong.D: The cone resists thrust along the axle, so it is structural, not ornamental.

commonMistakes: Answering the impression given in the previous sentence rather than the explanation the colon supplies.

whyCorrect: The passage shows the air, not the glass, setting the limit: more polishing does not help, and committees began spending a whole season testing the steadiness of the air on a ridge before laying a foundation. Behaviour like that means the site now matters as much as the telescope — the ground had become no less consequential than the instrument.

whyWrong.A: Cost is never compared. A railway is mentioned for convenience of access, not for expense.
whyWrong.B: Accessibility is what the committees stopped ranking first, so it is the criterion being displaced rather than the one being asserted.
whyWrong.C: Familiarity plays no part; an assistant camping on an untried ridge is the opposite of choosing what is known.

tips: When a passage describes a change in behaviour, the blank usually names what that behaviour shows people now believe.

whyCorrect: The mint really does keep the difference at first, so a gain exists. But "within a season" the heavy coin disappears into hoards or abroad and prices rise to match the new metal, which cancels the advantage. A gain that is real and then wiped out within a season is short-lived.

whyWrong.A: Legality is never raised; the crown itself is doing the debasing.
whyWrong.B: The passage describes market reactions — hoarding and price rises — not public disapproval.
whyWrong.D: "Imaginary" would mean no gain ever existed, but the passage says the mint kept the difference; the point is that the gain did not last.

commonMistakes: Reading "prices had risen to match" as proof the gain was never real, when the sentence begins by timing the reversal at one season.

whyCorrect: The passage distinguishes two counts: returning adults that bred before, and birds hatched three or four seasons earlier arriving to breed for the first time. It then says a colony losing adults faster than it gains those newcomers is in decline. "Recruitment" is the count of that second group — young birds joining the breeding population.

whyWrong.A: The military sense is the word's most familiar one, but no armed force appears in the passage.
whyWrong.C: Hiring staff is the workplace sense, again transferred from the same root; the subject here is seabirds on ledges.
whyWrong.D: Bringing in supplies is not a sense the passage supports; nothing is delivered to the colony.

tips: A technical sense of a common word is usually defined by the sentence immediately before it — read that sentence before the choices.

whyCorrect: Follow the order. First the material and its problems: two thousand volumes, contradictions, works surviving only in quotation. Then the compilation: a commission that cut, altered and rearranged. Then the result: a fiftieth of the bulk, reading as though the law had never been disputed. Description of the problem, the operation, and its outcome.

whyWrong.A: No later legal system is mentioned, so nothing is compared with Roman law.
whyWrong.C: The jurists are described only as authors of the material; no career is traced.
whyWrong.D: The last sentence notes what the compilation conceals but stops short of arguing the compilers were wrong to do it.

tips: For a structure question, label each sentence's job in order and match the sequence, not the topic.

whyCorrect: The passage ends with a measurement: the relation contains wavelength, angle and spacing, two of which can be measured directly so the third follows. The underlined sentence is what supplies that relation — the condition, in whole wavelengths of extra path, under which a sharp beam appears at all. Without it there is nothing to solve for the spacing.

whyWrong.B: Why X-rays scatter from electrons is never addressed; the sentence concerns when the scattered waves reinforce rather than cancel.
whyWrong.C: It raises no doubt about locating the beams; the rest of the passage relies on them being measurable.
whyWrong.D: No apparatus is described anywhere in the text.

commonMistakes: Treating a sentence full of physical detail as background, when the closing sentences depend on it directly.

whyCorrect: The passage contrasts two states. A hammered coin's irregular edge hides a paring, so clipping was common despite savage punishment. Machine striking put an even edge with a legend or grooves on it, and after that a clipped coin "announced itself" and would not pass at face value. The deterrent came from visibility, not from penalties.

whyWrong.B: The passage says severe punishment failed to make clipping rare, and it reports no increase in severity after the press.
whyWrong.C: Striking accuracy is the means, not the point; the main idea is what that accuracy did to clipping.
whyWrong.D: Output volume is never mentioned; the advantage described is the marked rim.

tips: When a passage says one remedy failed and another worked, the main idea is usually why the second one worked.

whyCorrect: The passage turns on one fact with two consequences: the ripening signal is a gas that moves between fruit. Because it spreads, a single over-ripe apple pulls a whole crate forward; because it can be removed or added, a store scrubs it to hold fruit back and admits it to bring a consignment on. The main idea has to cover both.

whyWrong.A: This reports one practice and leaves out both the mechanism and the deliberate ripening the store also performs.
whyWrong.C: The passage never compares how much ethylene different fruit give off; the point is that any is enough to spread.
whyWrong.D: This is the biochemical effect, a supporting detail rather than the idea the passage is organised around.

commonMistakes: Choosing a true sentence from one half of the passage when the main idea has to link the natural spread and the commercial control.

whyCorrect: Two things changed together, so the support has to separate them. This finding does exactly that by crossing the pairs: the modern fine-grid model given only 1980 observations is no better than 1980's forecasts, while the old coarse model given modern satellite data improves sharply. The gain travels with the observations, not with the grid.

whyWrong.A: That satellites supply most observations today shows their volume, not that they are what produced the improvement in accuracy.
whyWrong.B: A comparison between two-day and five-day forecasts says nothing about which of the two changes drove either one.
whyWrong.D: The size of modern grid cells quantifies the other candidate cause without weighing it against observations, so it does not favour Tveit.

tips: When two changes are confounded, the strongest evidence swaps one while holding the other fixed.

whyCorrect: Falcó says the log reads as a record of the air, with the observing programme entered only as what the air allowed. This entry is exactly that: the state of the atmosphere is described in detail, and the programme appears only as the work that had to be abandoned — the double-star sheets laid by until the air will carry them.

whyWrong.B: This concerns the instruments and a missing eyepiece, with no mention of the atmosphere at all.
whyWrong.C: Here the programme proceeds as planned and the air is never mentioned, which is the reverse of the claim.
whyWrong.D: A visitor being shown round is an administrative note and bears on neither the air nor the observing programme.

commonMistakes: Choosing an entry that mentions observing when the claim requires the air to be what governs whether observing happens.

whyCorrect: Løvold's claim is a trade-off, so the evidence must show one quantity rising as the other falls across the range. The table does: as speed goes 25, 100, 400, 1600, resolving power goes 200, 125, 80, 45. Naming the two extremes and stating that the fall holds at every step is what establishes the trade rather than a coincidence.

whyWrong.A: A single grain diameter with no speed or resolution beside it shows no relationship.
whyWrong.B: This compares two plates on resolving power alone and never mentions speed, so no trade-off is demonstrated.
whyWrong.C: That the process plate has the smallest grains is one column of one row; it says nothing about what speed costs.

tips: A claim about a trade-off needs both variables, moving in opposite directions, across more than one pair of rows.

whyCorrect: The passage says the separation of reflections is what allows an arrangement to be worked out, and that a powder superimposes reflections that a single crystal would have kept apart. So a powder cannot yield a structure from first principles, but it still gives a pattern — and a pattern can be matched against ones already recorded. That is what remains available.

whyWrong.A: One reflection's strength is far less than the passage allows; matching uses the whole pattern of positions and intensities, not a single peak.
whyWrong.C: This ignores the loss the passage has just described. Superimposed reflections are exactly what prevents a full solution.
whyWrong.D: The powder method is itself an X-ray method, so ruling out X-rays contradicts the passage.

commonMistakes: Treating the powder method as either fully equivalent to single-crystal work or useless, when the passage marks out a middle case.

whyCorrect: The wheel is held together by the iron tyre squeezing the wooden parts inward. The last sentence adds that wooden felloes shrink over a dry summer while the iron does not. If the wood inside shrinks and the hoop around it does not, the squeeze is lost and the joints the tyre had been holding closed go slack.

whyWrong.B: A firmer grip would require the wood to swell or the iron to contract; the passage says the reverse happens.
whyWrong.C: Swelling is the opposite of the shrinkage the passage describes for a long dry summer.
whyWrong.D: Load-carrying capacity is never discussed, and a loosened wheel would carry less, not more.

tips: Follow the physical relationship stated in the last sentence — which part changes size and which does not — before reading the options.

whyCorrect: Both halves are complete sentences: "A winemaker who wants a red to lose its edge encourages it" and "one who is making a crisp white in a warm region generally works to prevent it." No coordinating conjunction joins them, so a semicolon is required.

whyWrong.A: With nothing between them the two clauses fuse, and "encourages it one" reads as a single confused phrase.
whyWrong.B: A colon is not used with "and," and the second clause contrasts with the first rather than explaining it.
whyWrong.D: A comma between two independent clauses without a conjunction is a comma splice.

tips: Two parallel clauses set against each other still need a semicolon — parallelism does not license a comma.

whyCorrect: What follows the blank is a list spelling out the three timbers just referred to: elm for the hub, oak for the spokes, ash for the rim segments. The words before the blank form a complete sentence, and a complete sentence introducing a list takes a colon.

whyWrong.B: A comma would make "elm for the hub …" look like a continuation of the same clause rather than the enumeration it is, and it cannot carry the introducing force the sentence needs.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, but the list is a series of noun phrases with no verb.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation, "one for another elm" runs together and the list has no boundary marking its start.

tips: A complete statement followed by the items it promised takes a colon.

whyCorrect: "Cooling the crystal to a hundred kelvin before the exposure slows that damage by a large factor" is a complete sentence, and "cooling does not stop it altogether" is another. "However" is a conjunctive adverb and cannot join them, so a semicolon goes before it and a comma after.

whyWrong.A: With no mark before "however" the two clauses run together into a fused sentence.
whyWrong.B: A colon introduces an explanation or specification; here the second clause qualifies the first, and a colon is not used before a conjunctive adverb linking two clauses.
whyWrong.D: A comma before "however" produces a comma splice, since "however" cannot do a conjunction's work.

tips: Two independent clauses plus "however" always take a semicolon before it, never a comma.

whyCorrect: "Since" makes everything up to "its filament is unbroken" a subordinate clause, and the main clause is "growers stifle the pupae in hot air within a few days of spinning." An introductory subordinate clause is followed by a comma.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and a "Since" clause cannot stand alone.
whyWrong.B: A colon must follow a complete statement, which the "Since" clause is not.
whyWrong.C: "And" would try to coordinate a dependent clause with an independent one, leaving "Since" with nothing to attach to.

commonMistakes: Mistaking a long "Since" clause for a sentence because it contains several verbs; the subordinating word at the front settles it.

whyCorrect: The sentence describes a period that ended: four hundred years of dominance closed off by Japanese and Chinese silk displacing the Italian filatures in the 1870s. A finished stretch of past time takes the simple past, so "dominated" is right.

whyWrong.A: The present perfect "have dominated" implies the dominance reaches the present, but the passage says it ended in the 1870s.
whyWrong.C: "Will dominate" places the events in the future, contradicting the dates given.
whyWrong.D: The simple present "dominate" asserts a current state of affairs that the same sentence denies.

tips: An end date in the sentence rules out the present perfect — that tense needs the period to still be open.

whyCorrect: With a "neither … nor" subject the verb agrees with whichever element stands closer to it. Here the nearer element is "the commentary written upon them," which is singular, so the verb is singular. The time frame is past — before the sixth century — so it is "was collected."

whyWrong.A: "Have been" is plural and in the present perfect, implying a period running to the present, which "before the sixth century" rules out.
whyWrong.B: "Are" is plural and present tense; the sentence describes a state of affairs in antiquity.
whyWrong.D: "Were" is plural, agreeing with "the edicts" rather than with "the commentary," which is the element the verb actually follows.

tips: For "neither A nor B," find the noun immediately before the verb and match the verb to that one.

whyCorrect: The sentence fixes a point in the past — the first advertisement in 1878 — and describes testing that had already been going on for nearly three years before it. An action completed or continuing up to an earlier past point takes the past perfect, so "had been tested" is correct.

whyWrong.A: "Will be tested" is future, but the testing precedes an 1878 event.
whyWrong.B: "Is being tested" places the testing in the present, which cannot precede a point in 1878.
whyWrong.C: "Is tested" is simple present and states a general practice rather than a period ending at the stated past moment.

tips: "By the time" plus a past date is a reliable cue for the past perfect.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences establish that undetectably small differences grow until nothing is left in common, doubling in a day or two. The sentence after the blank draws the consequence: no better model or denser network can push a useful forecast much past a fortnight. That is a result, so a result transition is needed.

whyWrong.B: "Even so" would mean the fortnight limit holds despite the instability, but the instability is what imposes the limit.
whyWrong.C: "Similarly" claims a parallel, and the second statement follows from the first rather than matching it.
whyWrong.D: "For example" would present the forecast horizon as an instance of doubling errors, when it is what those errors imply.

tips: If the last sentence could begin "therefore," the blank wants a result transition.

whyCorrect: The first sentence names one obstacle — the timing information is destroyed and is needed to recover the structure. The second names a second obstacle of the same kind: the strengths are only relative and need a further step before they can be compared with calculated values. Two difficulties stacked up call for an additive transition.

whyWrong.A: "As a result" would make the relative scale a consequence of the lost timing, but the two are independent limitations of the same measurement.
whyWrong.B: "In short" introduces a summary, and the second sentence adds new information rather than condensing what came before.
whyWrong.D: "By contrast" needs opposition, but both sentences describe shortcomings pointing the same way.

commonMistakes: Reading any second problem as a contrast; problems that accumulate take an additive transition.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes rich soil producing excessive wood and leaf, with fruit ripening in its own shade — an unfavourable outcome. The second reports the best-known vineyards sitting on thin, stony ground. Two opposite soils set against each other require a contrast transition.

whyWrong.A: "Consequently" would make thin soils a result of deep soils growing too much canopy, which is not a causal link between two separate sites.
whyWrong.B: "For example" would offer the stony vineyards as an instance of deep, well-watered soil, which they are the opposite of.
whyWrong.C: "Likewise" claims the two sentences agree, but they describe opposite conditions.

tips: When two sentences describe opposite versions of the same variable, the transition is contrastive.

whyCorrect: The goal is about the vehicle as a whole, so the answer must go past the spring itself to what it let the builder remove. This choice does: the steel spring absorbs and returns instead of swinging as the braces did, and because it needs neither the posts nor the perch, the whole vehicle could be built lighter.

whyWrong.A: This describes the old arrangement only, with no change and no effect on the vehicle.
whyWrong.B: A patent and a date record when the spring appeared, not what it altered.
whyWrong.C: This states the weakness of the leather braces but stops before the new springs and the weight saved.

tips: When a goal says "as a whole," look for the choice that reaches the knock-on effect, not just the component that changed.

whyCorrect: The goal asks how the distance is covered without flapping, which needs the wind gradient, the manoeuvre, and the energy it yields. This choice supplies all three: friction slows the wind at the surface and it is faster higher up, the bird climbs, turns downwind and descends, and each crossing of the boundary gains airspeed — hence a thousand kilometres a day with hardly a wingbeat.

whyWrong.B: This gives the wind gradient alone and never says what the bird does with it.
whyWrong.C: This states the achievement the goal asks you to explain, without any explanation.
whyWrong.D: This describes the manoeuvre but omits why crossing between fast and slow air yields energy, which is the whole mechanism.

tips: An explanation of "how" must include the step that converts the condition into the result — here, the gain at each crossing.

whyCorrect: The goal asks what changed about the route a tune took into the archive, so the answer must show both the old route and the new. This choice sets the ear-and-staff-notation method, with its inability to record a pitch between two keys, against the cylinder, which keeps the performance as sung and allows a transcription to be checked back against it.

whyWrong.A: This states the limitation of notation only, with no mention of the phonograph or of what changed.
whyWrong.B: This states what a cylinder preserves but never contrasts it with the older practice the goal asks about.
whyWrong.D: This records when phonographs went into the field, which is a date rather than a change in how tunes were captured.

commonMistakes: Choosing the note that names the new technology when the goal asks what it changed, which always needs the before as well.
